changes.before:
The \ac{nrm} framework of \textcite{Xiong2026nrm}, developed by Ping Xiong, Thomas
Schnake, Grégoire Montavon, Klaus-Robert Müller, and Shinichi Nakajima, provides a
closely related view of the backward calculation. Its basic object is a
normalized signed measure on complete neuron walks. Relevance assigned to selected
neurons or concepts is obtained by summing over the walks passing through them;
conditional relevance is a ratio of joint and marginal relevance when the
conditioning relevance is nonzero. With suitable normalized propagation rules,
this includes ordinary \ac{lrp}, concept relevance, and Concept Relevance
Propagation (CRP)~\parencite{Achtibat2023CRP}. In particular, their CRP quantity is
the joint relevance of an input neuron, an intermediate concept neuron, and the
target output, rather than automatically a conditional probability.
changes.after: The \ac{nrm} framework of \textcite{Xiong2026nrm}, by Ping Xiong, Thomas Schnake, Grégoire Montavon, Klaus-Robert Müller, and Shinichi Nakajima, studies backward calculations through a normalized signed measure on complete neuron walks. Summing walk relevance through selected neurons or concepts gives their relevance; conditional relevance divides joint by nonzero marginal relevance. With suitable normalized propagation rules, this covers ordinary \ac{lrp}, concept relevance, and Concept Relevance Propagation (CRP)~\parencite{Achtibat2023CRP}. Their CRP quantity is joint relevance of an input neuron, intermediate concept neuron, and target output, without an automatic conditional-probability interpretation.
changes.preserved: All authors retained; signed complete-walk measure, ratio nonzero condition and CRP joint-versus-conditional distinction retained.

changes.before:
Both views therefore retain paths through the network before reducing them to
an attribution map. Their factorization supports sum-product computation and
queries involving neurons in several layers. The distinction is what a path
carries. In \ac{nrm}, walk relevance may be negative even though its total is one.
Here, the game policies define a non-negative probability law $\Pi$ on the expanded
state graph, including the player label and termination. Gradients and relevance
scores are recovered from signed differences of discounted occupation measures of this law
(Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory}); they are generally not its unweighted marginals.
The player expansion therefore separates trajectory probability from the sign
and scale of the backward contribution. It does not by itself identify $\Pi$
with a given \ac{nrm} measure.
changes.after: Both views retain network paths before forming attribution maps; their factorization supports sum-product computation and queries across layers. In \ac{nrm}, individual walk relevance may be negative despite unit total. Our game policies define a non-negative probability law $\Pi$ on the expanded graph, including player labels and termination. Signed differences of its discounted occupation measures recover gradients and relevance scores (Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory}), generally distinct from unweighted marginals. Player expansion thus separates trajectory probability from contribution sign and scale, without identifying $\Pi$ with a given \ac{nrm} measure.
changes.preserved: Preserves factorization, expanded-state structure, sign/scale recovery and non-equivalence.

requires the constant-sum conditions of \textcite[Section~3.5]{Xiong2026nrm}.
Our transition probabilities remain normalized while discounts retain the scale

changes.before:
Symbolic XAI scores logical feature queries by selecting signed contributions
from a decomposition of predictions into terms of multiple orders~\parencite{Schnake2025SymbolicXAI}.
SemanticLens combines component attributions with semantic embeddings to audit
alignment with expected and spurious visual concepts~\parencite{Dreyer2025SemanticLens}.
These query scores and semantic similarities address feature relationships and human
interpretation; our trajectory probabilities describe normalized routing.
We propose querying game trajectories through selected concepts, retaining signs
and discounts for attributions, and comparing their laws across inputs or models.
Equivalence with a particular \ac{nrm}/CRP construction would require matching
propagation rules, normalization, and absorption conventions; it remains unproved here.

These address feature relationships and human interpretation; trajectory probabilities describe normalized routing. changes.before:
The cascading-randomization sanity check of~\textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} asks whether an explanation
meaningfully depends on the learned parameters, and answers by comparing attribution maps in pixel
space. The object of interest here is the normalized backward routing---a distribution $\Pi$ over
graph trajectories. The attribution map is recovered through a model-dependent signed discounted
occupation projection of this law.
The \textbf{Hellinger distance}~\parencite{Hellinger1909} $\mathrm{H}(\Pi_A, \Pi_B) = (1 -
    \mathrm{BC})^{1/2}$, with Bhattacharyya coefficient~\parencite{Bhattacharyya1943} $\mathrm{BC} =
    \sum_\zeta \sqrt{\Pi_A(\zeta)\,\Pi_B(\zeta)}$, measures the routing logic directly rather than its
visual projection. This section probes the representation claim: parameter randomization should
move $\Pi$ even when the resulting attribution map remains stable. We remark that $\mathrm{H}=0$ iff $\Pi_A
    = \Pi_B$, and the metric takes its maximal value $\mathrm{H}=1$ iff their supports are disjoint.
Unlike KL-type divergences, $\mathrm{H}$ stays finite when randomization opens or closes routes,
and since both laws are layered Markov chains on the same state graph, BC factorizes along layers:
one backward pass computes $\mathrm{H}$ exactly, in time linear in the number of edges, and
$\mathrm{H}^2$ decomposes into per-input-state contributions (Section~\ref{ptnb:app:path-divergence}).
changes.after:
The cascading-randomization sanity check of~\textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} tests explanations' dependence on learned parameters by comparing pixel-space maps. Here we examine normalized backward routing: a trajectory distribution $\Pi$ whose model-dependent signed discounted occupation projection recovers attribution.
The \textbf{Hellinger distance}~\parencite{Hellinger1909} $\mathrm{H}(\Pi_A, \Pi_B) = (1 -
    \mathrm{BC})^{1/2}$, with Bhattacharyya coefficient~\parencite{Bhattacharyya1943} $\mathrm{BC} =
    \sum_\zeta \sqrt{\Pi_A(\zeta)\,\Pi_B(\zeta)}$, directly compares routing. We test whether parameter randomization moves $\Pi$ even when attribution maps remain stable. The metric satisfies $\mathrm{H}=0$ iff $\Pi_A = \Pi_B$ and $\mathrm{H}=1$ iff their supports are disjoint. It remains finite when routes open or close, unlike KL-type divergences. For layered Markov laws on the same graph, BC factorizes: one backward pass computes $\mathrm{H}$ exactly in edge-linear time, and $\mathrm{H}^2$ decomposes into per-input-state contributions (Section~\ref{ptnb:app:path-divergence}).
changes.preserved: Retains model-dependent projection, exact metric extremes, support mismatch behavior, same-state-graph assumption, linear computation.

This subsection puts the trajectory-space machinery to two empirical tests, holding the model
fixed: how the Hellinger trajectory distance reacts to input perturbations, and whether the
resulting distance separates inputs from different ImageNet-S classes from one another and from

kernel~\eqref{ptnb:eq:rg-T-act} at $\tau = 1$.
The diagnostic Routing-Game kernel omits the bias action and renormalizes the remaining branches, so it can differ from the bias-inclusive attribution game.

changes.before:
\textbf{Can the Hellinger distance differentiate between inputs of different classes?} Partly; the
reference baselines in Table~\ref{ptnb:tab:hellinger-input-random} make the answer architecture- and
kernel-specific:
\begin{itemize}
    \item On \textbf{VGG-16}, the \ac{sg} $\mathrm{H}$ is the kernel that does the work: clean-intraclass
        $\mathrm{H}=0.513$ sits below clean-interclass $\mathrm{H}=0.607$. The \ac{rg} kernel saturates at
        $\mathrm{H}=1$ on every row on VGG-16, so it cannot resolve class structure on this architecture.
    \item On \textbf{ResNet-50}, the \ac{rg} kernel is the discriminating one: clean-intraclass
        $\mathrm{H}=0.786$ vs.\ clean-interclass $\mathrm{H}=0.902$. The \ac{sg} kernel does not separate
        classes on ResNet-50 (intraclass $0.272$ vs.\ interclass $0.268$).
    \item On \textbf{ViT-B/16}, the \ac{rg} kernel gives intraclass $0.789$ vs.\ interclass $0.882$; the
        \ac{sg} gap ($0.422 \pm 0.023$ vs.\ $0.435 \pm 0.017$) is smaller than the spread over pairs, so
        the \ac{sg} does not separate classes there.
\end{itemize}
Random-vs-random is the lowest row in every column whose rows differ, and clean-vs-random is the
highest row of every plain-$\mathrm{H}$ column except the \ac{sg} on ResNet-50 ($0.269$ vs.\
intraclass $0.272$) and the saturated \ac{rg} on VGG-16, consistent with the model routing Gaussian
inputs differently from in-distribution images. The conditioned variant
$\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{surv}}$ is at least $0.99$ on every row of VGG-16 and ResNet-50 and for the
\ac{rg} on ViT-B/16, so it carries no class-separability signal there. For the \ac{sg} on ViT-B/16
it separates random-vs-random ($0.852$) from the clean rows ($0.957$--$0.968$), but neither
intraclass from interclass pairs ($0.963$ vs.\ $0.968$) nor clean-vs-random ($0.957$) from the
clean pairs.
changes.after:
Class separation depends on architecture and kernel (Table~\ref{ptnb:tab:hellinger-input-random}):
\begin{itemize}
    \item On \textbf{VGG-16}, \ac{sg} gives clean-intraclass $\mathrm{H}=0.513$ below clean-interclass $\mathrm{H}=0.607$. \ac{rg} saturates at $\mathrm{H}=1$ throughout, resolving no class structure.
    \item On \textbf{ResNet-50}, \ac{rg} separates clean-intraclass $\mathrm{H}=0.786$ from clean-interclass $\mathrm{H}=0.902$; \ac{sg} does not (intraclass $0.272$ vs.\ interclass $0.268$).

changes.starts_with: We adapt the cascading parameter randomization test
changes.before:
We adapt the cascading parameter randomization test of \textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} to the attribution
methods of Table~\ref{tab:sanity-check}. Starting from a pretrained network, we cumulatively
re-initialize the convolutional and linear layers from the output toward the input (weights Kaiming
normal~\parencite{He2015delving}, biases $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2)$); BatchNorm (ResNet-50) and
LayerNorm, the positional embedding and the class token (ViT-B/16) keep their pretrained values.
The ViT attribution cascade includes the decomposed query/key/value linear projections; the
Hellinger cascade of Section~\ref{ptnb:sec:hellinger-cascading} retains the packed query/key/value
parameters. At each randomization depth we compute the attribution for
every test image under both the original and the (partially) randomized model, then measure the
similarity between the two attribution maps. The test asks whether attribution maps change as
learned parameters are randomized; it does not require similarity to decrease monotonically with
randomization depth. Persistent similarity can indicate dependence on input structure or
architectural properties.
changes.after: We apply the cascading randomization test of \textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} to Table~\ref{tab:sanity-check}'s attribution methods. Starting pretrained, we cumulatively re-initialize convolutional and linear layers output-to-input: weights Kaiming normal~\parencite{He2015delving}, biases $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2)$. BatchNorm (ResNet-50), LayerNorm, positional embeddings, and class token (ViT-B/16) retain pretrained values. The ViT attribution cascade randomizes decomposed query/key/value projections; the Hellinger cascade (Section~\ref{ptnb:sec:hellinger-cascading}) retains packed query/key/value parameters. At each depth, we compare original and randomized models' attributions for every test image. The test asks whether maps change, without requiring monotonic similarity decay. Persistent similarity can reflect input structure or architecture.

changes.starts_with: We report two complementary similarity measures
changes.before:
We report two complementary similarity measures between attribution maps:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Spearman $\rho(|a|)$}: The Spearman rank correlation of the absolute attribution values,
        measuring whether the two maps rank pixels in the same order of importance. We use absolute values
        because sign conventions may differ between original and randomized attributions; the correlation
        itself is signed.
    \item \textbf{HOG $r$}: The Pearson correlation between Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG)
        descriptors~\parencite{Dalal2005hog} extracted from the attribution maps, capturing structural
        similarity at the level of local gradient orientations.
\end{itemize}
We do not report SSIM here. The remaining similarity scores are complementary diagnostics:
\textcite{Binder2022shortcomings} show that input-dependent structure and activation scales can
survive top-down randomization, and that low similarity can also reflect noise. Their noise
critique also applies to Spearman correlation, including ranks of absolute attribution values.
All values are averaged over the 565-image test split of ImageNet-S (50 classes); a map that is
constant over the image (LIME and KernelSHAP on ResNet-50 at the cascade endpoint, whose output no
longer depends on the superpixels) has similarity $0$ by convention. Table~\ref{tab:sanity-check}
reports the similarity at the \emph{cascade endpoint} (all tested convolutional and linear layers
re-initialized, with the pretrained parameter groups listed above retained).

output at the cascade endpoint no longer depends on the superpixels and their maps are constant

changes.before:
The within-Hellinger block shows that per-image $\mathrm{H}$ carries a stable ordering of the
images. Where little trajectory mass reaches the cemetery, the plain and conditioned distances of
the same game rank images almost identically: $\rho = +0.96$ (\ac{rg}) and $+0.99$ (\ac{sg}) on
ViT-B/16, and identical values for the \ac{rg} on VGG-16, whose kernel routes no trajectories to
states of dead neurons. Under the \ac{sg} on the \ac{relu} backbones the two normalizations
decouple ($\rho = -0.30$ on VGG-16, $+0.16$ on ResNet-50): the cemetery share of plain $\mathrm{H}$
varies with the image's dead masks, and the renormalization by $1/\sqrt{Z_A Z_B}$ removes exactly
this share. The conditioned distances of the two games agree strongly on the \ac{relu} backbones
($\rho = +0.85$ on VGG-16, $+0.89$ on ResNet-50) and only weakly on ViT-B/16 ($+0.28$), where the
two kernels read partly different per-image structure.
changes.after: Within Hellinger, per-image $\mathrm{H}$ gives a stable ordering. When little mass reaches the cemetery, plain and conditioned distances rank images almost identically: $\rho = +0.96$ (\ac{rg}) and $+0.99$ (\ac{sg}) on ViT-B/16. VGG-16 \ac{rg} gives identical values because it never routes to dead-neuron states. For \ac{sg} on \ac{relu} backbones, the normalizations decouple ($\rho = -0.30$ VGG-16, $+0.16$ ResNet-50): image-dependent dead masks change the cemetery share, which renormalization by $1/\sqrt{Z_A Z_B}$ removes. The two games' conditioned distances agree strongly on \ac{relu} backbones ($\rho = +0.85$ VGG-16, $+0.89$ ResNet-50), but weakly on ViT-B/16 ($+0.28$), where the kernels capture partly different per-image structure.
